This makes ACR the correct choice even though tubing sizes are still specified in inch fractions on the job.

front: Why must copper tubing be cut with a proper tubing cutter instead of a hacksaw?
back: A hacksaw introduces metal filings into the tube that a rotary cutter wheel avoids entirely. Those filings can travel through the system and damage components. A tubing cutter also produces a cleaner, more consistently round cut for proper fitting seating.

front: A technician advances a tubing cutter with heavy pressure in one pass to save time. What is wrong with this?
back: The cutter wheel should be advanced gradually, a quarter turn at a time, rotating the cutter fully around the tube between advances. Rushing the cut with heavy pressure produces a pinched, oval end instead of a round one. An out-of-round cut will not seat properly in a fitting and can leak.

front: Why must a tube end be deburred after cutting, and how should the mechanic hold the tube while reaming?
back: An un-reamed tube restricts flow at the joint, and the burr can shear off during operation and travel downstream to plug a metering device or valve seat. Deburring must remove the burr fully while keeping the tube round. The mechanic should tip the tube downward while reaming so shavings fall out rather than into the tube.

front: Why is brazing the primary method for permanently joining refrigerant piping?
back: A properly brazed joint is stronger than the tube itself and, unlike a mechanical fitting, has no gasket or seal that can degrade over time. The filler metal fuses tube and fitting into a continuous piece of metal with effectively no leak path. Its main weakness is that it cannot be reasonably disassembled without cutting the joint out.

front: Why does the fit-up gap between tube and fitting socket matter for a brazed joint?
back: A brazed joint relies on capillary action drawing molten filler metal into the small clearance between the tube and the fitting socket. Too loose a fit and capillary action fails, leaving voids in the joint. Too tight a fit and the filler cannot penetrate the joint at all.

front: Why should mating surfaces before brazing be abraded with emery cloth rather than steel wool?
back: Steel wool leaves fine particles that contaminate the copper and can initiate corrosion. Emery cloth or sandpaper cleans the surface without leaving that contamination behind. Clean, dry surfaces are essential because any oxide, oil, or moisture prevents the filler from wetting the base metal properly.

front: Why is flux not required when brazing a copper-to-copper joint with phos-copper filler?
back: Phosphorus-bearing filler alloy, commonly called Phos-Copper, acts as a self-fluxing agent on copper because its phosphorus content shields the surface during heating. Flux is only necessary when brass or steel is part of the joint. Those base metals get no benefit from the phosphorus self-fluxing effect and will oxidize rapidly under heat without a flux coating.

front: A mechanic is brazing a copper line to a brass service valve. Does this joint need flux?
back: Yes, flux is required whenever brass or steel is part of the joint, such as copper-to-brass service valves or copper-to-steel adapters. These base metals do not benefit from the phosphorus self-fluxing effect that copper-to-copper joints get from Phos-Copper filler. Flux should be applied sparingly with a brush, only to the area to be heated, to avoid contaminating the system.

front: During brazing, where should the torch heat be directed first, and where should the filler rod be introduced?
back: Heat is directed first at the base of the fitting socket and moved around the joint to bring both tube and fitting to a uniform temperature. The filler rod is then introduced at the joint mouth, not directly into the flame. The filler should flow into the joint by capillary action and form a smooth, continuous fillet around the full circumference.

front: What internal problem does nitrogen purging during brazing prevent, and how does it work?
back: When copper is heated with oxygen and moisture trapped inside the pipe, a black internal oxide scale forms on the inner wall, which later breaks loose and can plug filter driers, score compressor bearings, and contaminate the oil. Dry nitrogen fed through the piping at a low flow rate displaces the oxygen inside the tube so no internal oxidation can occur. Flow should continue before, during, and after brazing until the joint has cooled enough that oxidation is no longer possible.

front: Where are flare joints used instead of brazed joints, and why?
back: Flares are used almost exclusively where a joint must be serviceable, meaning it may need to be disconnected in the field. Examples include service valves on compressors and condensing units, some sight glasses, and line-set connections for ductless split systems. These locations need connections made and broken routinely during commissioning or service.

front: A mechanic flares a tube end and then realizes the flare nut is still in the toolbox. What went wrong?
back: The flare nut must be slid onto the tube before flaring begins. This is a step that is easy to forget, and forgetting it forces the mechanic to redo the flare since the nut cannot be added afterward. Producing a good flare also starts with a square, deburred cut.

front: Why does the tube stick-up in a flaring block matter when producing a flare?
back: The tube is clamped in the flaring block with the stick-up specified by the tool manufacturer. Too much stick-up produces an oversized flare that cracks, and too little stick-up produces an undersized flare that will not seat. Getting the stick-up right is essential to a leak-free, serviceable joint.

front: What should a mechanic check before assembling and torquing a completed flare joint?
back: The flare should be checked visually for a uniform cone with no cracks before the joint is assembled and torqued to specification. Overtightening the flare nut can also crack the flare, so torque should be applied to specification rather than by feel. A cracked or malformed flare will leak under pressure.

front: What is swaging, and what advantage does it offer over a standard coupling fitting?
back: Swaging expands the end of one tube so a second tube of the same nominal size can be inserted directly into it without a coupling fitting, and the joint is then brazed. This produces a joint with fewer components and one less potential leak point than a standard coupling. A swaging tool expands the tube in stages to avoid splitting the copper.

front: How deep should a swaged tube end be expanded relative to the inserted tube's OD?
back: The swaged depth should equal or slightly exceed the outside diameter of the tube being inserted. This gives adequate surface area for the braze to form a strong, capillary-fed joint. A swaging tool expands the tube gradually in stages to avoid splitting the copper.

front: Why does sagging refrigerant piping between supports cause a problem beyond appearance?
back: Sagging creates low points where oil pools and unwanted traps form along the run. This disrupts intended oil return and can starve other parts of the system of lubrication. Supports must be spaced closely enough to prevent this sagging while still letting the pipe move without stress concentrating at any one point.

front: How does support spacing differ between small flexible tubing and larger rigid pipe?
back: Horizontal runs are supported at regular intervals, tighter for smaller, more flexible tubing and wider for larger, rigid pipe. Additional support is added near every change of direction and near heavy in-line components such as filter driers or solenoid valves. This prevents the weight of those components from hanging on the tubing alone.

front: What two things absorb compressor vibration so it does not fatigue the connected rigid piping?
back: Compressors are typically mounted on rubber-in-shear or spring isolators at the base. The lines connecting to the compressor should include a flexible connector or vibration eliminator hose, plus at least one 90 degree offset or loop in the rigid piping nearby. Together these absorb cyclic vibration rather than carrying it straight down a stiff run.

front: A pipe clamp is installed rigidly very close to the compressor discharge line. Why does this defeat the vibration isolation?
back: Rigid clamps installed too close to the compressor defeat the isolators and flexible hose entirely, because vibration simply finds another rigid path through the clamp. The flexible connector and offset loop only work if the piping near the compressor is otherwise free to flex. This can fatigue the pipe and transmit noise through the building structure over time.

front: Why is a sleeve used where refrigerant piping passes through a wall, floor, or roof?
back: A sleeve keeps the pipe from being clamped directly by the structure at the penetration. This allows the necessary thermal movement of the pipe as it expands and contracts with temperature. It also keeps vibration from transferring into the building structure.

front: Why do vertical suction risers pose a greater oil return challenge than horizontal suction lines?
back: On horizontal suction lines, gas velocity alone is usually enough to keep oil moving along with the refrigerant. On vertical risers, gravity constantly pulls oil back down the pipe wall, so refrigerant velocity has to be high enough to carry it upward against gravity. If design velocity is too low, oil accumulates at the base of the riser instead of returning to the compressor.

front: What happens if oil accumulates at the base of a vertical suction riser due to low velocity?
back: The oil eventually forms a slug that can hit the compressor and cause serious mechanical damage. In the meantime, the compressor is starved of the lubrication it needs since the oil is not returning with the refrigerant. This is why riser velocity design is critical, not just a comfort issue.

front: What is the function of a trap placed at the base of a vertical suction riser?
back: The trap collects any oil that has fallen out of suspension in a small pocket at the base of the riser. As gas continues to move past, it periodically picks that oil back up and carries it upward. This prevents the oil from simply pooling indefinitely at the base of the riser.

front: How often should additional traps be placed on a tall vertical suction riser?
back: Additional traps are placed at intervals up a tall riser, generally every 6 to 8 metres or per the manufacturer's engineering data. Re-entrained oil can fall out of suspension again over a long run. Periodic traps keep picking that oil back up rather than letting it pool over a long vertical distance.

front: What oil return problem does capacity modulation create for a single fixed-size suction riser?
back: A riser sized for full-load velocity will be oversized at minimum load, and velocity at low capacity may drop below the minimum needed to carry oil upward at all. This happens when a compressor runs at reduced capacity through unloading or staging. A single riser cannot maintain adequate oil-carrying velocity across the full range of capacity.

front: Compare how gas flows through a double riser at minimum load versus at increased load.
back: At low load, all gas is forced through the small riser at high velocity, which keeps oil moving properly despite the low flow. As load and gas volume increase, a trap arrangement between the two risers lets gas flow through the larger pipe as well, once there is enough volume to maintain adequate velocity in both. This keeps oil return effective across the full range of capacity rather than at one design point alone.

front: Compare the leak path and strength of a properly made brazed joint versus a mechanical flare or compression fitting.
back: A properly made brazed joint is permanent and extremely strong, with effectively no leak path since the filler fuses tube and fitting into a continuous piece of metal. A flare or compression fitting relies on a mechanical seal that can loosen from vibration, thermal cycling, or age. Brazed joints cannot be reasonably disassembled, while mechanical fittings can be disconnected and reconnected without heat.

front: Name two situations where a flare or compression fitting is the correct choice over a brazed joint.
back: They are correct for service valves and for connections a technician will realistically need to service equipment behind, since they can be disconnected without heat. They are also correct where hot work is not practical or permitted, such as close to combustible material or in an occupied space where a fire watch cannot reasonably be arranged. A brazed joint would require cutting out the pipe to service these connections.

front: What must a mechanic do at every service visit specifically because of how mechanical joints fail?
back: Every mechanical joint must be checked at every service visit because the mechanical seal can loosen from vibration, thermal cycling, or age. This is the tradeoff for the convenience of being able to disconnect and reconnect the joint without heat. A brazed joint does not carry this same ongoing inspection requirement since it has no seal to loosen.

front: What governs where mechanical joints are permitted on a refrigeration system, beyond convenience or speed?
back: Provincial and national codes generally restrict where mechanical joints may be used, particularly in concealed locations or high-pressure applications. A mechanic must know the code requirements for the jurisdiction and refrigerant involved. Choosing between mechanical and brazed joints is a design and code decision, not just a matter of convenience.

front: Name the two reasons suction lines and other cold surfaces must be insulated.
back: Insulation reduces heat gain into the refrigerant, which would otherwise cost system efficiency. It also prevents surface condensation on the cold pipe, which left unmanaged leads to dripping water damage and, over time, ice buildup on the pipe. Both reasons apply to any pipe surface running below the ambient dew point.

front: Compare closed-cell elastomeric insulation to fiberglass insulation for refrigeration piping.
back: Closed-cell elastomeric insulation is now the standard for refrigeration piping because its structure resists moisture absorption almost entirely. Fiberglass is open-cell and will absorb and hold moisture if its outer jacket is ever breached, which loses most of its insulating value and can accelerate corrosion of the pipe underneath. Fiberglass is now seen mainly on larger commercial ductwork rather than piping.

front: What happens if a vapour barrier around insulated suction line piping is breached by a gap or puncture?
back: Warm, moist ambient air reaches the cold pipe surface underneath the insulation, where it condenses and, on very cold suction lines, freezes. That trapped moisture cannot escape once inside the insulation, so it accumulates over time. The resulting ice can eventually split the insulation jacket open.

front: How should seams and butt joints in elastomeric insulation be sealed, and what is the common mistake?
back: All seams and butt joints must be sealed with the manufacturer's specified contact adhesive, applied to both mating surfaces and allowed to become tacky before joining. The common mistake is pressing the surfaces together dry instead of using adhesive. A continuous vapour barrier is the part of the installation most often done poorly.

front: At a penetration, hanger, or support, how must insulation be treated to maintain the vapour barrier?
back: At every penetration, hanger, support, or transition to a fitting, the insulation must be sealed back to itself or to a boot fitting. There must be no break in the vapour barrier anywhere along the run. Any single gap allows moisture to reach the cold pipe underneath.

front: What gas is used for pressure testing refrigeration piping, and what must never be used instead?
back: Pressure testing uses dry nitrogen, brought up to a standing test pressure appropriate to the system's design pressure and applicable code. Oxygen and compressed air must never be used for this purpose. The test pressure is held for a specified period, commonly hours, while the technician watches for any drop on a calibrated gauge.

front: During a standing pressure test, what factor besides an actual leak can cause the gauge reading to change?
back: Ambient temperature change affects gauge pressure independent of any leak, so the technician must account for it when reading the gauge over the test period. A confirmed drop beyond what temperature explains indicates a real leak. Only after the system holds pressure with no unexplained drop should nitrogen be released and evacuation begin.

front: A pressure test shows a confirmed gauge drop not explained by temperature change. What is the next step?
back: A confirmed drop indicates a leak that must be located, commonly with an electronic detector or soap bubble solution at every joint. The leak must be repaired before proceeding. Only after the system holds pressure with no drop should nitrogen be released and evacuation begin.

front: What is deep vacuum theory, and why does it justify pulling a system down to microns rather than kPa?
back: At very low absolute pressure, measured in microns of mercury rather than kPa or psig, the boiling point of any residual water drops low enough that it boils off as vapour and is pulled out by the vacuum pump. This is the mechanism behind evacuation removing air, nitrogen, and moisture from the system. A coarse gauge reading in kPa cannot show whether this deep a vacuum has actually been reached.

front: Why is a single evacuation often not sufficient to fully dry out a refrigeration system?
back: Moisture can be trapped in oil, in fittings, or adsorbed onto internal surfaces in a way that does not release completely on the first vacuum pass. A single evacuation may leave this trapped moisture behind even though the gauge shows a deep vacuum was reached. This is the reason the triple evacuation method is used instead.

front: Describe the steps of the triple evacuation method.
back: The system is pulled to a deep vacuum, then broken with dry nitrogen back up to a slight positive pressure, which helps release trapped moisture. This cycle repeats three times before the final deep evacuation is held. Each nitrogen break disturbs residual moisture that the previous vacuum pass could not reach directly.

front: Why should a micron gauge be installed away from the vacuum pump rather than right at it?
back: A reading taken too close to the pump can show a deeper vacuum than actually exists elsewhere in the system, due to pressure drop across long hoses or restrictive fittings. Installing the gauge away from the pump gives a reading that reflects the true vacuum level in the piping being evacuated. A standard compound gauge is not accurate enough at these pressures, so a micron gauge is required.

front: How is a rate-of-rise test performed after evacuation, and how does the technician interpret the result?
back: The technician isolates the system from the pump and observes the micron gauge over ten to fifteen minutes. A slight rise that levels off is attributable to residual moisture still evaporating and is generally acceptable. Pressure that climbs steadily without leveling off indicates a leak letting outside air back in, which must be found and repaired before evacuation and charging proceed.

front: How should a liquid receiver be mounted, and where does the liquid line take suction from?
back: Liquid receivers are typically mounted vertically with proper support for their weight when full, since they store excess refrigerant charge. They are positioned so the liquid line takes suction from the bottom of the receiver. This ensures liquid refrigerant, not vapour, is drawn out to feed the rest of the system.

front: What does a suction accumulator protect against, and how does trapped oil get back to the compressor?
back: A suction accumulator protects the compressor from liquid or oil slugging during abnormal conditions such as low load or defrost. It is piped with the correct internal oil-return orifice or U-tube so oil trapped inside meters back to the compressor rather than sitting indefinitely. Correct orientation of this internal metering feature is essential to its function.

front: What two things does a sight glass let a technician visually confirm?
back: A sight glass lets the technician visually confirm a full column of liquid, where bubbles indicate an undercharge or restriction in the system. Many sight glasses also include a moisture indicator that changes colour to warn of contamination. Together these give a quick visual check of charge and moisture condition.

front: Why should a filter drier be installed only after brazing is complete on that section of piping?
back: Installing the drier before brazing that section would let scale and flux residue from the brazing process immediately load the drier. Installing it after brazing keeps the drier's capacity available for normal system contaminants instead. The drier must also be installed with its arrow pointing in the direction of flow.

front: What installation requirement applies specifically to a solenoid valve's coil?
back: The coil must be oriented as specified by the manufacturer, typically upright. The flow arrow on the valve body must also be matched correctly to the actual system flow direction. Solenoid valves control flow electrically, so correct coil orientation is necessary for the internal mechanism to operate as designed.

front: What structural loads must a rooftop condensing unit's mounting pad or curb be rated to support in most of Canada?
back: The pad or curb, whether concrete, rubber isolation pads, or an engineered roof curb, must support the full operating weight of the unit plus wind load and, in most of Canada, snow load. Roof-mounted equipment also needs proper flashing and curb sealing to prevent water infiltration at the penetration. Enough clearance must also be left for airflow and service access.

front: State Ohm's Law and its two rearranged forms for finding current and resistance.
back: Ohm's Law is V = I x R, where V is voltage, I is current, and R is resistance. Rearranged for current, I = V / R. Rearranged for resistance, R = V / I. A technician who can shuffle all three forms can diagnose most control circuit faults with just a multimeter and a schematic.

front: A 24V relay coil has 60 ohms of resistance. Find its power draw using P = V squared / R.
back: P = V squared / R = 24 squared / 60 = 576 / 60 = 9.6W. This is the same coil power that could also be found as P = V x I once current is known from I = V / R.

front: A 24V transformer secondary feeds a contactor coil drawing 0.3A. Find the coil's resistance and power draw.
back: Using R = V / I: R = 24V / 0.3A = 80 ohms. Using P = V x I: P = 24V x 0.3A = 7.2W. These are the coil's normal healthy operating values.

front: With power off, a contactor coil that should read 80 ohms instead measures 400 ohms. What does this tell a technician?
back: The coil is likely partially failed and will not pull in reliably, even though it still shows some resistance instead of reading open. A healthy coil at that rated voltage and current should measure close to 80 ohms. This kind of drifted but not open reading is easy to miss if a technician checks only for continuity instead of an actual resistance value.

front: A compressor start winding draws 15A locked rotor through a winding resistance of 2 ohms. Find the power using P = I squared x R.
back: P = I squared x R = 15 squared x 2 = 225 x 2 = 450W. This is the heat the winding must dissipate during a locked rotor moment, which is why a protector responding to actual winding temperature matters during a prolonged locked rotor event.

front: A 240V defrost heater has a resistance of 9.6 ohms. Calculate the current draw using I = V / R.
back: I = V / R = 240V / 9.6 ohms = 25A. This current value would be checked against the heater's nameplate rating and the circuit's overcurrent protection to confirm both are sized correctly.

front: Compare series and parallel circuit behavior, and explain how control circuits typically combine both.
back: In series, current is the same everywhere and voltage divides across each resistance, so total resistance is the sum of the parts. In parallel, voltage is the same across every branch and current divides, so total resistance is always lower than the smallest branch. Most control circuits wire switches and interlocks in series, so any one open contact stops the circuit, while loads are sometimes wired in parallel so each gets full line voltage independently.

front: Describe single phase power supply and how its waveform behaves over one cycle.
back: Single phase power is what most Canadian residences receive, typically 120V and 240V split phase, with one alternating current waveform. That waveform rises and falls to zero twice per cycle. Small residential condensers, furnace blowers, and light commercial rooftop units under a certain tonnage commonly run on single phase.

front: Describe three phase power and list common three phase supply voltages used in this trade in Canada.
back: Three phase power delivers three separate alternating waveforms, each offset by 120 electrical degrees, so the waveforms never all cross zero at the same instant. Common Canadian three phase supply voltages in this trade include 208V, 347/600V, and 575V, depending on the utility service and building type.

front: Why do commercial and industrial refrigeration systems typically use three phase power instead of single phase?
back: Because the three waveforms never all cross zero together, three phase delivers smoother, more continuous torque than single phase. This reduces mechanical stress on bearings and windings, improves starting under load, and lets a smaller conductor carry more power than single phase at the same voltage. Compressors above roughly five horsepower are typically three phase for these reasons.

front: A newly installed scroll compressor runs backward, draws abnormal current, and makes unusual noise. What is the likely cause?
back: The incoming three phase legs are connected in the wrong sequence, since scroll compressors are direction sensitive. Running backward, the compressor also fails to build pressure differential. Rotation direction should always be verified on every new three phase compressor before it is left running unattended.

front: How does a technician correct a three phase compressor that is rotating backward?
back: Swap any two of the three incoming legs, or use a phase sequence meter to confirm correct sequence before connecting. This corrects the reversed rotation caused by wrong phase sequence. Verifying rotation direction on every new three phase installation prevents leaving a backward-running compressor unattended.

front: Describe a permanent split capacitor (PSC) motor and where it is commonly used.
back: A PSC motor wires a run capacitor permanently in series with the start winding, staying in the circuit the entire time the motor runs. This gives moderate starting torque and good efficiency with few parts to fail. PSC motors are the most common single phase motor in residential condenser fans and many blowers.

front: Describe a capacitor-start capacitor-run (CSR) motor and why it suits compressors that start against pressure.
back: A CSR motor adds a start capacitor, switched in only during starting through a potential or current relay, then dropped out near 75 percent of running speed. This gives much higher starting torque than a PSC motor alone. CSR motors are common on reciprocating and older scroll compressors that must start against system pressure.

front: Compare PSC and CSR motors in terms of starting torque and typical application.
back: A PSC motor uses one run capacitor permanently in the circuit, giving moderate starting torque and fewer parts to fail. A CSR motor adds a start capacitor that switches in only during starting and drops out near 75 percent speed, giving much higher starting torque. CSR is chosen when the motor must start against system pressure, while PSC suits lighter starting loads like condenser fans.

front: How does a three phase induction motor produce torque without needing a capacitor?
back: The three phase supply itself creates a rotating magnetic field in the stator, which induces current in the rotor and produces continuous torque from start to run. No run or start capacitor is needed, unlike single phase PSC or CSR motors. This is one reason three phase motors are generally more reliable than single phase capacitor motors of similar horsepower.

front: What is an electronically commutated motor (ECM), and how is its speed controlled?
back: An ECM is a brushless DC motor controlled by an onboard module that converts incoming AC to DC and electronically switches polarity to the windings. Instead of running at one fixed speed, an ECM ramps speed smoothly to a control signal. The module, not line voltage directly, sequences energization of the windings.

front: Why should a technician never apply line voltage directly to an ECM's winding leads?
back: An ECM's onboard module must sequence energization to the windings correctly, and line voltage applied straight to the leads can destroy the motor instantly. ECMs also run around 60 percent more efficiently than PSC motors, which is a separate reason they are increasingly common. Both facts matter when diagnosing or replacing an ECM.

front: Compare external overload protectors and internal thermal (klixon) protectors on a compressor motor.
back: An external overload mounts outside the shell, often bolted to the terminals, opening the circuit when current exceeds a calibrated threshold, usually sensed via a bimetallic disc responding to current heat. An internal thermal protector is embedded inside the windings, so it responds to actual winding temperature rather than a value measured at the terminal. This makes internal protectors more accurate against a genuine overheating winding during a brief locked rotor spike or a slow overheat from poor airflow.

front: A compressor won't start, but continuity from common to run and common to start is normal, with none to the shell. What's the likely cause?
back: The windings are likely intact, so the fault is probably elsewhere, such as a protector still cooling, a failed capacitor, or a control circuit fault. Most overload protectors reset automatically once cooled, which is why a compressor tripped on internal overload may restart on its own minutes or hours later with no technician intervention. This behavior confuses many apprentices chasing an intermittent no run complaint.

front: What is a contactor, and what two factors determine its rating?
back: A contactor is an electrically operated switch that uses a low voltage control signal to control a high current or high voltage load, such as a compressor or condenser fan. Its coil is energized by the 24V control circuit, magnetically pulling contacts closed. It is rated by coil voltage, typically 24V, and by contact current rating, which must meet or exceed the running and locked rotor current of the equipment switched.

front: Compare a relay and a contactor, and explain why reading a relay's contact symbols matters.
back: A relay uses the same electromagnetic principle as a contactor but generally handles lighter loads, such as switching one low voltage signal to another or interlocking parts of a control sequence. Some relays use normally open contacts, some normally closed, and some both. Reading the schematic symbol correctly is essential to predicting what the relay actually does when its coil energizes.

front: What is a thermostat, and what are its two basic sensing designs?
back: A thermostat is a temperature sensitive switch that opens or closes a control circuit based on sensed temperature. It can be mechanical, using a bimetallic element or sealed bellows, or electronic, using a thermistor and microprocessor. Most thermostats switch the 24V control circuit rather than line voltage.

front: Compare what a high pressure switch and a low pressure switch each protect against.
back: A high pressure switch protects against excessive discharge pressure, which could rupture components or signal a condenser airflow problem. A low pressure switch protects against very low suction pressure, indicating lost charge, a restriction, or an icing evaporator. The low pressure switch also prevents compressor operation against a near vacuum, since suction gas cools the motor on many designs.

front: What does an anti-short-cycle timer do, and why does a compressor need one?
back: An anti-short-cycle timer prevents a compressor from restarting for roughly three to five minutes after it stops. This protects the compressor from starting against unequalized high side pressure. Without this delay, a quick call for cooling right after shutdown could force the compressor to start under abnormal load.

front: Compare fan-on delay and fan-off delay in a time delay relay's function.
back: A fan-on delay holds the blower off until a heat exchanger has warmed, preventing a blast of cold air at the start of a heating call. A fan-off delay keeps the blower running briefly after the heat call ends, extracting residual heat from the exchanger before shutdown. Both improve comfort and efficiency by timing fan operation to actual heat exchanger temperature.

front: Why must a technician read a relay's normally open versus normally closed symbol correctly before predicting circuit behavior?
back: A relay's contacts can be normally open, normally closed, or a mix of both on the same relay. Misreading which type a given contact is leads to a wrong prediction of what happens when the coil energizes, since a normally open contact closes on energizing while a normally closed contact opens. Correctly reading the schematic symbol is essential to accurately predicting the resulting circuit state.

front: How is current traced through a rung on a ladder diagram?
back: A ladder diagram shows two vertical power rails with individual circuits drawn as horizontal rungs between them. Reading left to right along a rung traces the current path: a power source on the left rail, through switches and interlocks in series, to a load such as a coil, and back to the other rail. This lets a technician see exactly which conditions must all be true for a load to energize.

front: Describe the standard ladder diagram symbols for a normally open contact, a normally closed contact, and a coil.
back: A normally open contact is two short parallel lines with a gap between them. A normally closed contact adds a diagonal slash through that gap. A coil is drawn as a circle or an elongated oval, and these symbols appear consistently across manufacturers with only minor variation.

front: A cooling contactor's rung wires the thermostat contact, both pressure switches, and a timer contact in series. What happens if any one opens?
back: The whole rung loses continuity and the contactor de-energizes, even though the thermostat still calls for cooling. A technician who checks only the thermostat will miss the actual fault, since any single open interlock in that series string stops the entire circuit. This is why tracing every device on the rung matters, not just the obvious one.

front: How does a 24V control transformer connect into a residential control circuit, and what is terminal C for?
back: The transformer's primary connects to line voltage, either 120V or 240V, and its secondary delivers 24V. One secondary leg, C for common, is the return path for the entire control circuit, connecting to the C terminal at both the equipment board and the thermostat. The other secondary leg, R (or Rc/Rh), feeds the thermostat.

front: What happens at the thermostat and equipment when a call for cooling connects R to Y?
back: Connecting R to Y sends 24V to energize the compressor contactor, and on many systems the outdoor fan relay as well. This is the standard cooling call terminal in a 24V control circuit. The Y wire routes from the thermostat back to the equipment board's Y terminal, with the coil's other side returning to C.

front: What happens when a call for the indoor fan connects R to G?
back: Connecting R to G energizes the blower relay, or on an ECM-equipped system, the ECM module's fan call input. This is the standard fan call terminal in a 24V control circuit, independent of a heating or cooling call. G is commonly energized alongside Y during a cooling call or W during a heating call, depending on system design.

front: What is terminal W used for, and what does a heat pump's O or B terminal control?
back: W is the heating call terminal, connecting R to W to energize gas valves, electric heat relays, or auxiliary heat. Heat pumps add an O or B terminal for the reversing valve, energized in either heating or cooling mode depending on manufacturer convention. That convention must be confirmed before assuming which mode energizes the reversing valve.

front: How does a technician verify correct 24V control circuit wiring with a multimeter?
back: Measure roughly 24 to 30V AC across R and C at the idle thermostat first. Then confirm each call, such as Y, G, or W, produces 24V between its terminal and C at the equipment end when that call is active. This confirms both the transformer secondary and the individual call wiring are functioning correctly.

front: Describe a run capacitor: its rating units, typical voltage, and duty cycle.
back: A run capacitor is rated in microfarads (uF, often printed as MFD) for continuous AC duty, commonly at 370V or 440V. It stays connected the entire time the motor runs, shifting the phase of current in the start winding relative to the run winding to produce a rotating field from a single phase supply. Values commonly range from around 5uF for a small condenser fan up to 40uF or more for a compressor.

front: Describe a start capacitor: how its microfarad rating compares to a run capacitor, and its duty cycle.
back: A start capacitor is often five to ten times higher in microfarads than a run capacitor, but rated for intermittent duty only at a lower voltage band. It connects only during starting, through a start relay, then disconnects near running speed. Leaving it connected continuously would overheat and destroy it quickly.

front: Compare a run capacitor and a start capacitor in terms of duty cycle and when each is in the circuit.
back: A run capacitor is rated for continuous duty and stays connected the entire time the motor runs. A start capacitor is rated for intermittent duty only, connecting through a start relay just during starting and disconnecting near running speed. A start capacitor left connected continuously would overheat and fail quickly, unlike a run capacitor.

front: What is a dual run capacitor, and how are its two values marked?
back: A dual run capacitor combines two microfarad values in one can, serving both the compressor and the condenser fan from a single component. The can is marked HERM for the compressor value and FAN for the fan motor value. This is a common space-saving design in residential condensing units.

front: How does a technician test a run or start capacitor, and what do a zero reading versus a near-zero reading indicate?
back: With power disconnected and the capacitor discharged by shorting its terminals with an insulated tool, connect a multimeter's capacitance function across the terminals and compare the reading against the label value, allowing for the printed tolerance, often plus or minus 6 percent. A reading of zero means the capacitor has failed open. A reading showing continuity like a closed switch, or very low ohms, means it has shorted internally and must never be reenergized, since it can draw damaging current or rupture the can.

front: What does a variable frequency drive (VFD) do to an AC motor's speed?
back: A VFD electronically varies the frequency and voltage supplied to an AC motor, letting speed adjust smoothly instead of running only at the fixed speed set by line frequency. Internally, it rectifies fixed frequency AC input to DC, then electronically synthesizes a variable frequency AC output sent to the motor. This lets one motor run across a range of speeds instead of only on or off.

front: How does changing frequency above or below 60Hz affect a VFD-driven motor's speed?
back: Reducing frequency below the standard 60Hz slows the motor, while increasing frequency above 60Hz, within the motor's limits, speeds it up. This relationship is the basic mechanism behind a VFD's speed control. Standard 60Hz is the reference point utility power is normally supplied at in Canada.

front: Name two common applications of VFDs in refrigeration and HVAC equipment and their main benefit.
back: VFDs increasingly control compressor speed directly, matching capacity to actual load rather than cycling a fixed speed compressor on and off, improving part load efficiency substantially. They are also common on condenser fans and larger air handling fans, where reduced speed during mild weather or lower ventilation demand saves energy compared to dampers throttling a fixed speed fan. Both applications trade fixed on/off cycling for smoother, load-matched operation.

front: A VFD-driven compressor will not run. What should a technician check first, and what special cabling consideration applies?
back: Check the VFD's fault code display first, since it is usually the fastest diagnostic starting point rather than immediately suspecting the motor itself. VFD output is not the same clean sine wave as utility power, so VFD-fed motors and cables sometimes need specific cable types to manage electrical noise. A conceptual understanding of these two points is enough for most service work.

front: What does bonding accomplish on refrigeration and HVAC equipment, and why does it matter for safety?
back: Bonding connects normally non current carrying metal parts, such as an equipment frame or compressor shell, together and to the system ground. This gives a fault that energizes the frame a low resistance path back to the source, letting enough current flow to trip overcurrent protection quickly. Without bonding, a fault could leave the frame energized at a dangerous voltage instead of tripping a breaker or fuse.

front: How does grounding differ from bonding, even though the two are often confused?
back: Grounding connects the electrical system to earth, mainly for lightning and surge protection and to stabilize system voltage relative to earth potential. Bonding instead connects equipment metal parts together and to ground so a fault has a low resistance path to trip overcurrent protection. These are distinct purposes even though the two terms are frequently used interchangeably by mistake.

front: Under CSA C22.1, how must the bonding conductor for a piece of fixed HVAC equipment be installed?
back: Every piece of fixed equipment must have its exposed metal frame bonded with a conductor sized to the overcurrent device protecting the circuit, per the CEC's bonding conductor sizing tables. That conductor must be continuous, with no breaks or unauthorized splices, and it cannot rely on mechanical contact alone. CSA C22.1 is the Canadian Electrical Code that governs this requirement for equipment installed in Canada.

front: What does CSA C22.1 require regarding a disconnecting means for HVAC and refrigeration equipment?
back: A disconnecting means must be within sight of, and readily accessible to, the equipment, rated for the circuit's voltage and current. Under provincial lockout and tagout practice, it must be able to accept a physical lock so it cannot be re-energized while a technician is working. Disconnects are commonly a pull-out block, a knife blade switch, or a breaker style disconnect mounted at or near the equipment.

front: After opening a disconnect, why should a technician still test for zero energy before touching exposed conductors?
back: A mislabeled disconnect or a wiring error elsewhere can leave a supposedly de-energized circuit still live, even though the disconnect appears open. A properly rated multimeter should verify zero energy at the equipment terminals after opening the disconnect. Testing rather than trusting the disconnect's position alone is the only way to confirm the circuit is actually safe to touch.

front: What is the correct three-step sequence for systematic electrical troubleshooting?
back: Start with a visual inspection for burnt wiring, discoloured or melted terminals, a bulged capacitor, a tripped breaker, or a blown fuse. Next, perform voltage checks, starting at the disconnect and working downstream to confirm power is present where expected. Finally, with power disconnected and locked out, perform continuity or resistance checks on the suspect components this narrows down to.

front: Voltage is present at a contactor's line side but absent at its load side while the coil is energized. What does this indicate?
back: The contactor's contacts have likely failed, since the coil is pulling in but current is not passing through to the load side. This differs from voltage being absent at the line side itself, which would instead point to a fault upstream, such as a blown fuse. Voltage checks worked in sequence from source to load isolate exactly where in the circuit the fault sits.

front: Why might a resistance check catch a compressor winding fault that a simple continuity check would miss?
back: A continuity check only shows whether a path is open, reading infinite resistance or OL on many digital meters, or complete, not whether the resistance value is normal. A resistance check compares the measured value against specification or a known good component, which can reveal a partially shorted or open winding that still shows some continuity. This makes resistance checks especially useful on compressor, transformer, and motor windings.

front: Why should every terminal in the disconnect, contactor, and compressor terminal box be physically checked with a screwdriver at startup, not just visually inspected?
back: Vibration during shipping and handling loosens factory electrical connections even when they look intact. A loose terminal can arc and destroy a compressor winding within the first thirty seconds of run time, so mechanical tightness must be confirmed by hand, not by sight alone.

front: Why must three-phase equipment with a scroll compressor be checked with a phase rotation meter before startup?
back: Scroll compressors are direction sensitive. Wired backward, a scroll compressor runs hot and loud but never develops a real pressure differential, so confirming correct phasing before energizing prevents a startup that looks like it is running but is not actually pumping refrigerant.

front: What is the typical acceptable tolerance between supply voltage and compressor nameplate voltage before startup?
back: Supply voltage should match nameplate voltage within about plus or minus 10 percent. A reading outside that band should be investigated and corrected before the compressor is brought online, since sustained under voltage or over voltage stresses the motor windings.

front: What position should king valves and compressor service valves be in for normal operation before startup, and why does gauge port capping matter?
back: They should be fully back-seated for normal operation with gauge ports capped. A valve left cracked or a port left uncapped can leak refrigerant continuously or send liquid the wrong direction, so the pre-startup walkthrough confirms every valve position, not just that the valves exist.

front: What eventually happens to a refrigerant line set that is not supported at code-required intervals?
back: An unsupported line set vibrates continuously during operation. Over time that vibration work-hardens the metal at the joints, and the line eventually fractures, so proper support spacing is confirmed visually during the pre-startup walkthrough.

front: During pre-startup verification, what specifically must be confirmed about high and low pressure cutouts, beyond their physical presence in the panel?
back: The cutouts must actually be wired into the control circuit, not merely installed in the panel. A safety device sitting unwired will not stop the compressor when a dangerous pressure condition occurs, so wiring continuity is checked, and the high pressure setpoint is confirmed against the refrigerant in use.

front: What is the typical minimum crankcase heater warm-up time before first startup for larger commercial compressors versus smaller residential units?
back: Larger commercial compressors typically need a minimum of 12 to 24 hours of crankcase heater warm-up, while smaller residential units need several hours, always per manufacturer instructions. This warm-up must occur before line voltage is applied for the first startup or after any extended period without power.

front: Why is a micron gauge used to confirm evacuation instead of the compound gauge on the manifold set?
back: The compound manifold gauge loses meaningful resolution long before the vacuum gets deep enough to boil off residual moisture. A micron gauge is the only field instrument accurate enough to confirm the system reached the deep vacuum target required before charging.

front: What vacuum level do CSA and manufacturer specifications typically require before charging a standard commercial or residential system?
back: The system should be pulled down to about 500 microns, roughly 0.5 mmHg or about 0.02 inHg vacuum. Larger commercial or low-temperature systems often carry a tighter target than this standard 500-micron benchmark.

front: Once the target vacuum is reached, why should the vacuum pump be isolated with a valve rather than simply switched off?
back: A pump left connected while shutting down lets air migrate backward through its oil as the pump cools. Isolating the pump at the core tool or a manifold valve seals the system off cleanly so the rate-of-rise test reflects the system alone, not the pump.

front: During a rate-of-rise vacuum test, the micron reading climbs from 500 to about 1,200 microns, then levels off and holds. What does this indicate?
back: A rise that levels off and holds after climbing is normal residual moisture outgassing, not a leak. The system can proceed to charging once the reading stabilizes, since this pattern is expected on nearly every properly evacuated system.

front: During a rate-of-rise vacuum test, the micron reading climbs steadily without leveling off, continuing back toward atmospheric pressure. What does this indicate?
back: A reading that keeps climbing without leveling off indicates an actual leak in the system, not moisture outgassing. The leak must be located and repaired, and the system re-evacuated, before any refrigerant is introduced.

front: Name at least five measurements that belong in a complete baseline commissioning data record besides suction and discharge pressure.
back: A complete baseline record also includes suction line temperature and calculated superheat, liquid line temperature and calculated subcooling, compressor amp draw on each leg against nameplate rated load amps, voltage at the compressor terminals under load, ambient outdoor and return air temperature, and supply air temperature split across the coil. The date, mechanic's name, and conditions present at the time are recorded alongside the readings themselves.

front: When is a triple evacuation with nitrogen breaks between pulls recommended instead of a single standard vacuum pull?
back: It is recommended whenever moisture contamination is suspected, such as after a compressor burnout recovery or on a system left exposed to atmosphere for an extended period. Breaking nitrogen between pulls, or pulling a single extended vacuum well below 500 microns, gives far higher confidence than one quick pump-down on a contaminated system.

front: When is weighing in a refrigerant charge by mass the correct charging method, rather than superheat or subcooling?
back: Weigh-in is used whenever the equipment nameplate or installation manual specifies an exact charge weight, typically on a factory-charged split system near its base line set length, or after a full recovery where a known quantity must be replaced. It is the most accurate method available when a specified target mass exists.

front: How is a factory-specified charge weight adjusted for a split system whose line set is longer than the manufacturer's base length?
back: The mechanic adds a manufacturer-specified correction, commonly expressed as a certain number of grams per metre of additional liquid line beyond the base length. The scale under the charging cylinder is zeroed first so the mechanic can charge to the total corrected mass accurately.

front: The superheat method for verifying charge applies to which type of metering device, and why?
back: It applies to fixed-orifice metering devices, meaning piston or capillary tube systems with no active feedback control over refrigerant flow. Because the orifice cannot respond to load changes, correct charge is defined by hitting a target superheat cross-referenced against a manufacturer chart for the actual conditions.

front: State the formula for calculating superheat at the evaporator outlet, and identify the two measurements it requires.
back: Superheat equals the actual suction line temperature minus the saturation temperature. The line temperature comes from a clamp-on probe at the evaporator outlet, and the saturation temperature comes from converting measured suction pressure using a pressure-temperature chart for the refrigerant in use.

front: On a fixed-orifice system, measured suction pressure converts to a saturation temperature of 2°C. The clamp-on probe at the evaporator outlet reads 9°C. Calculate superheat.
back: Superheat equals actual line temperature minus saturation temperature, so 9°C minus 2°C equals 7°C of superheat. That figure is then compared against the manufacturer's superheat chart for the current indoor and outdoor conditions to judge whether the charge is correct.

front: If a measured superheat reading is lower than the manufacturer's target, is the system overcharged or undercharged, and what corrects it?
back: A lower than target superheat means the system is overcharged, since adding refrigerant lowers superheat by letting more liquid reach the coil before it fully boils off. The correction is to remove refrigerant in small amounts until superheat rises back to the target.

front: The subcooling method for verifying charge applies to which type of metering device, and why is superheat not used there instead?
back: It applies to systems using a thermostatic expansion valve (TXV) or electronic expansion valve (EXV). Because these devices actively regulate superheat at the evaporator outlet regardless of charge level within a reasonable range, superheat readings become useless for judging charge, so subcooling at the condenser outlet is used instead.

front: State the formula for calculating subcooling at the condenser outlet, and identify the two measurements it requires.
back: Subcooling equals the saturation temperature minus the actual liquid line temperature. The saturation temperature comes from converting measured high side liquid line pressure using a pressure-temperature chart, and the actual temperature comes from a clamp-on probe at the condenser outlet.

front: An R-410A TXV system shows liquid line pressure converting to 45°C saturation temperature, with the liquid line thermometer reading 34°C. Calculate subcooling.
back: Subcooling equals saturation temperature minus actual line temperature, so 45°C minus 34°C equals 11°C of subcooling. Against a manufacturer target of 8°C, this reading is 3°C high, indicating the system is overcharged.

front: On a TXV system with an 8°C subcooling target, a stable reading comes back at 11°C. What corrective action does the mechanic take, and how?
back: Because the system is overcharged, the mechanic recovers small amounts of refrigerant in stages, letting the system stabilize between each removal. Refrigerant is removed gradually until subcooling reads 8°C at stable operating conditions, avoiding overcorrection from removing too much at once.

front: On a TXV system with an 8°C subcooling target, a stable reading comes back at 4°C. What does this indicate, and how is it corrected?
back: A 4°C reading is 4°C below the 8°C target, indicating the system is undercharged. The correction runs opposite to the overcharge case: the mechanic adds refrigerant in small metered amounts, letting the system stabilize between additions, until subcooling climbs to 8°C.

front: List the order of steps a mechanic follows once crankcase warm-up, oil, and pre-startup checks are complete, up to compressor startup.
back: The mechanic confirms disconnect is on and control voltage is present, confirms the thermostat or controller is calling correctly, then brings the compressor online while watching suction and discharge pressures for a normal rise and stabilization pattern. The mechanic also listens for abnormal noise in the first thirty seconds and confirms the condenser fan and evaporator blower are both running in correct rotation and airflow direction.

front: When is charging refrigerant as a vapour into the low side suction line the correct and safe practice?
back: Vapour charging into the suction line is standard for small trim adjustments on a system that is already running, because the vapour is simply compressed along with the rest of the suction gas. It carries no risk of liquid slugging as long as the compressor is actively pulling refrigerant through the line.

front: When is charging refrigerant as a liquid required rather than vapour, and through which service port?
back: Liquid charging is required for a large initial charge into an empty or nearly empty system, and it is done through the high side liquid line or king valve port with the compressor off. It is also faster than vapour charging for large quantities.

front: Why must liquid refrigerant never be charged into the suction side of a compressor that is not running?
back: Liquid entering the suction line of a stopped compressor pools in the crankcase instead of flashing to vapour. The instant that compressor starts, the pooled liquid causes a slugging event, which can bend connecting rods or shatter valve plates on the very first startup.

front: What is a zeotropic blend, and name three examples used in refrigeration and air conditioning.
back: A zeotropic blend is a mixture of refrigerant components with different boiling points, which causes it to exhibit temperature glide rather than boiling or condensing at a single fixed temperature. R-410A, R-407C, and R-448A are all zeotropic blends.

front: What is fractionation, and why does it happen when a zeotropic blend is charged as a vapour off the top of the cylinder?
back: Fractionation is the preferential evaporation of the lower-boiling-point component of a blend, leaving the cylinder's remaining refrigerant with a different composition than what left the factory. Charging vapour draws off the lighter component first, so the last portion of that cylinder throws off the system's designed pressure-temperature relationship and capacity.

front: Regardless of whether a system's charging point is high side or low side, how must every cylinder of zeotropic blend refrigerant be charged?
back: Every cylinder of zeotropic blend refrigerant must be charged as a liquid, drawn from the bottom of an upright cylinder or through a dip tube. A dedicated liquid charging device, or simply inverting a cylinder without a dip tube, are both accepted field methods to guarantee a liquid draw and avoid fractionation.

front: Describe the correct technique for purging air from a manifold gauge hose before connecting it to a system's refrigerant circuit.
back: With the gauge set connected to the refrigerant source and the service port, the mechanic briefly cracks the appropriate manifold valve to let a short burst of refrigerant push air out through the far hose's Schrader depressor fitting, directed away from the technician. The valve is then closed immediately, since skipping this step introduces air and moisture into the system with every connection made.

front: What advantage does a digital gauge set have over an analog gauge set during charging?
back: A digital gauge set lets the refrigerant type be selected electronically and displays saturation temperature directly alongside pressure, removing the risk of reading the wrong refrigerant scale on an analog dial. When temperature probes are connected, it also calculates superheat and subcooling automatically, reducing the chance of a manual chart-reading error.

front: What should be done with manifold gauge hoses at the end of a charging procedure, and under what regulatory framework?
back: Hoses are recovered into the low side briefly before disconnecting, minimizing the refrigerant trapped in the hoses that would otherwise vent to atmosphere. This practice is consistent with regulations under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act and provincial equivalents governing refrigerant handling.

front: During charging, which manifold valve is opened when trimming vapour into a running system, and which is opened when charging liquid into an off system?
back: The low side valve is opened when trimming vapour into a running system's suction line, and the high side valve is opened when charging liquid into an off system's liquid line. Both manifold valves stay closed except for whichever one is actively being used for the procedure underway.

front: On a fixed-orifice piston system, what happens if the installed piston is undersized versus oversized for the equipment tonnage?
back: An undersized piston starves the evaporator, producing high superheat and low system capacity. An oversized piston floods the evaporator, producing low superheat with a real risk of liquid returning to the compressor, so the correct piston size must be confirmed against the manufacturer's sizing chart at startup.

front: If a piston system's charge is correct by weight but superheat still reads out of spec, what should the mechanic suspect first, and why?
back: Piston systems have no field adjustment beyond the fixed orifice size itself. An out-of-spec superheat reading on a properly charged system usually points back to airflow, a wrong piston size, or a restriction elsewhere in the circuit, not the charge.

front: On a TXV with a field-adjustable superheat setting, which direction does the mechanic turn the stem to raise target superheat, and which to lower it?
back: Turning the stem clockwise in small increments, typically a quarter turn, raises the target superheat. Turning it counterclockwise lowers the target superheat, and the seal cap is removed and replaced using the small tool supplied with the valve.

front: Why does a mechanic wait ten to fifteen minutes between each TXV adjustment instead of making several quick turns in a row?
back: TXVs respond slowly to a stem adjustment, so the system needs time to restabilize before the effect of one change can be accurately judged. Overcorrecting from impatience, by adjusting again before the previous change has settled, is a common startup mistake.

front: On a properly subcooled TXV system, what is the typical target superheat range once the valve is correctly adjusted?
back: Target superheat on a properly subcooled TXV system typically falls between 5°C and 8°C, roughly 9°F to 14°F. Once subcooling and superheat both land in range together, the system is considered correctly charged with the valve correctly adjusted.

front: Compare polyolester (POE) oil and mineral oil use in refrigeration compressors, and explain why the two must never be mixed.
back: POE oil is used with HFC refrigerants such as R-410A and R-407C, while mineral oil remains compatible with older HCFC systems. Mixing the two is never acceptable because POE oil is highly hygroscopic and reacts differently with system materials than mineral oil does, so the correct oil type must match the compressor manufacturer's specification exactly.

front: What does a crankcase heater actually prevent, and what happens to a compressor started without adequate warm-up time?
back: The crankcase heater keeps compressor sump oil warmer than the surrounding refrigerant, preventing refrigerant vapour from migrating into the oil and condensing there during the off cycle. Without warm-up, dissolved refrigerant in a cold sump flashes to vapour violently at startup, foaming the oil and causing liquid slugging in the cylinders or scroll set, which destroys more new compressors during commissioning than almost any other mistake.

front: What is the approximate conversion between CFM and L/s, and which unit is still most commonly called out on a Canadian jobsite?
back: 1 CFM equals roughly 0.47 L/s. Even though L/s is the proper SI unit and appears on newer drawings, CFM remains the number techs call out to each other in the field, for example over a two-way radio during a rooftop unit test.

front: Compare a rotating vane anemometer to a hot wire anemometer for grille airflow readings.
back: A rotating vane anemometer measures velocity directly at a grille and that reading is multiplied by the grille's free area to get CFM. A hot wire anemometer performs the same job but responds better at low velocities, which matters at wide-throw diffusers where a vane anemometer can stall.

front: A tech reads grille velocity with a vane anemometer but has no free area value for the grille. Why is the reading useless?
back: CFM is calculated by multiplying velocity by the grille's effective free area, so without that area figure the velocity number cannot be converted into an airflow value. The free area is usually printed on the manufacturer's data plate or found by looking up the model number.

front: What is a duct traverse and when is it preferred over a single grille reading?
back: A duct traverse uses a pitot tube connected to a manometer to take velocity pressure readings across a grid of points on a straight duct run, then averages them and applies the cross-sectional area for a total CFM figure. It is far more reliable than a single-point reading taken near a fitting, elbow, or damper where airflow is turbulent.

front: Name the two standard grid methods used to lay out pitot tube traverse points across a duct cross-section.
back: The log-Tchebycheff method and the equal-area method are the two standard traverse grid layouts. Both give the tech a defined set of points to sample so the averaged velocity pressure represents the whole cross-section rather than one arbitrary spot.

front: What does total external static pressure (TESP) tell a mechanic, and what unit does a Canadian commissioning report typically use for it?
back: TESP shows how hard the fan is working to push air through the ductwork, filters, coils, and diffusers, and it is measured with a manometer connected to a static pressure tip. Canadian commissioning reports increasingly specify pascals (Pa) as the primary unit rather than inches of water column.

front: TESP on a rooftop unit reads higher than the design value on the fan curve. What are the most common causes?
back: A high TESP reading usually means something downstream is restricting airflow. Common causes include a dirty filter, a closed or partially closed damper, or an undersized duct run creating extra resistance.

front: TESP reads lower than design on a commissioned unit. What should the mechanic suspect?
back: A lower than design TESP suggests the fan is not seeing the resistance it was sized to overcome. This points to a duct leak or a damper stuck open that is bypassing part of the system's intended resistance.

front: Explain the proportional balancing method for adjusting supply air dampers across a zone.
back: The tech balances the branch closest to the fan first, then works outward toward the farthest branches. This produces a more stable result than chasing individual outlets randomly, because closing any one damper shifts pressure and airflow to the rest of the system.

front: Why does a mechanic need to confirm which flow unit a hydronic drawing set uses before recording balancing numbers?
back: Hydronic flow is measured in either GPM (US gallons per minute) or L/s depending on the project, and the two units are not interchangeable without conversion. Recording readings in the wrong assumed unit would make the whole balancing report inaccurate.

front: What is a calibrated balancing valve (circuit setter) and how does it produce a flow reading?
back: A calibrated balancing valve has a built-in venturi or orifice with pressure ports on either side of the restriction. A differential pressure reading across those ports is converted to a flow rate using the valve manufacturer's chart or an electronic balancing meter.

front: Compare balancing a two-pipe reverse-return hydronic system to balancing a direct-return system.
back: A reverse-return system is more forgiving because its piping geometry is already designed to equalize resistance across branches. A direct-return system usually needs more aggressive valve adjustment at the near end to create enough resistance that the far end still receives its full design flow.

front: A chilled water coil is designed for a 5.5°C delta-T but shows only 2°C under full load. What does this usually indicate?
back: A delta-T well below design under full load usually means flow through that coil is too high relative to its capacity. That excess flow robs delta-T from the rest of the loop and forces the chiller to work harder than necessary.

front: Why does the proportional balancing approach require re-checking earlier hydronic settings as later terminals are adjusted?
back: Adjusting a valve at one terminal changes the pressure differential across the whole loop, which shifts flow at terminals that were already set. Re-checking earlier settings after later ones are adjusted is necessary to keep the whole loop at its design flow values.

front: Before performance verification testing begins, what documents should the mechanic have in hand?
back: The mechanic needs the original mechanical drawings, the equipment schedule, and the manufacturer's performance data. These give the design values that measured readings will be compared against, rather than a generic rule of thumb.

front: List the key measurements compared against the equipment schedule during a refrigeration system performance verification.
back: Comparisons include suction and discharge pressures converted to saturation temperatures, superheat and subcooling, entering and leaving air or water temperatures at the evaporator and condenser, and total capacity calculated from measured airflow and coil temperature split. Every figure is checked against the equipment schedule's stated design condition.

front: Why is it a mistake to compare a system's readings on a mild day directly against its full design load numbers?
back: A system running at partial load on a cool day will naturally show different readings than one operating at full design load. Comparing readings taken under different operating conditions against the full-load design numbers leads to false conclusions about system performance.

front: A compressor motor is pulling amperage close to its nameplate FLA rating even though the system is at partial load. What does this signal?
back: Amperage that is high relative to the actual load usually points to a problem such as a mechanical binding issue, incorrect belt tension, or a refrigeration side fault forcing the compressor to work harder than the load requires. It should be checked against nameplate FLA and the design engineer's expected running amps.

front: Measured discharge air temperature does not match the design value. List the possible root causes a mechanic should work through.
back: Possible causes include an incorrect refrigerant charge, airflow across the coil being too low, the outdoor test condition not matching the equipment schedule's rating condition, or the equipment having been sized incorrectly at the design stage. Documenting which cause applies, with supporting readings, is what separates real verification from just recording numbers.

front: Why can a pressure gauge that reads 35 kPa low be worse than an obviously broken gauge?
back: A gauge that is off by a fixed amount can either send a mechanic chasing a problem that does not exist or hide a real problem because the readings happen to look acceptable on paper. An obviously broken gauge, by contrast, gets replaced immediately rather than trusted.

front: What calibration interval do most instrument manufacturers specify as a minimum for field instruments like manifold gauges and manometers?
back: Most manufacturers specify an annual calibration interval as a minimum. Some critical instruments need more frequent checks depending on how hard they are used, since mechanical shock, temperature extremes, and sensing element age all cause drift.

front: Describe a quick field check a mechanic can run to verify a pressure gauge before connecting it to a system.
back: The gauge should read zero at atmospheric pressure before it is connected to any system. This simple check does not replace a proper calibration certificate but catches a badly drifted gauge before it produces readings that end up in a formal report.

front: What two reference points can a mechanic use in the field to check a temperature probe without lab equipment?
back: An ice bath provides a known 0°C reference point, and boiling water provides a known 100°C reference point at sea level, adjusted for altitude. Checking the probe against both catches a significantly drifted sensor before it is trusted for reporting.

front: What instrument information must a commissioning report record, and why does this matter for a later warranty dispute?
back: The report should list the make, model, and serial number of every instrument used, along with the date of its most recent calibration. This protects the technician by demonstrating the readings were collected with instruments known to be accurate at the time of the test, not whatever gauge happened to be in the truck.

front: Why is sound measured on the A-weighted scale (dBA) rather than an unweighted decibel scale during commissioning?
back: The A-weighted scale approximates how the human ear actually perceives loudness across different frequencies. Readings are taken at specified locations, often the centre of an occupied space at standard height, and compared against the project's stated NC or RC rating.

front: An office space has a design sound target of NC 30 to NC 35. Does this target also apply to the mechanical room?
back: No. A mechanical room has no such restriction because it is not an occupied space, unlike the office area where the NC or RC target is meant to protect occupant comfort.

front: List the common root causes of a vibration complaint on refrigeration or air conditioning equipment.
back: Common causes are an unbalanced fan or compressor, a coupling misalignment, a failed or improperly selected vibration isolator, or resonance where the equipment's operating frequency matches a natural frequency of the supporting structure. A vibration meter measures velocity or acceleration at key points to identify which is at fault.

front: A rooftop unit is well balanced mechanically but the building still reports vibration transmitted into the structure below. What should the mechanic inspect first?
back: The mechanic should inspect the isolation devices, since a spring isolator that is bottomed out or a rubber mount that has hardened with age will transmit vibration directly into the structure. No amount of adjusting the equipment itself will fix a problem that is actually in the isolation.

front: What is the sequence of operations, and why can hardware that works perfectly still fail commissioning?
back: The sequence of operations is the written logic describing how the system should behave under every condition, including startup, normal operation, unoccupied setback, alarm conditions, and safety shutdowns. If the controls do not execute that logic correctly, the system fails commissioning even if every piece of hardware is functioning.

front: Give three examples of safety interlocks a mechanic must verify while testing sequence of operations.
back: Examples include a low pressure cutout actually stopping the compressor, a high discharge temperature limit actually shutting down the unit, and a proof-of-flow switch actually preventing compressor startup when water flow is not established. Each interlock has to be forced into its trigger condition to confirm it responds correctly.

front: A BAS graphic shows a different supply air temperature than the equipment's own controller display. What does this mismatch usually mean?
back: A mismatch between BAS points and the equipment's own readings usually means a sensor calibration issue or a wiring or addressing error at the BAS integration point. It needs to be resolved before handover, since a facility operator relying on inaccurate BAS data will make wrong decisions about the equipment.

front: Why are BAS trend logs valuable evidence in a commissioning report beyond a single spot-check reading?
back: A trend log, such as supply air temperature holding steady through a full occupied cycle or a chiller cycling at a reasonable frequency, gives documented proof the system behaves correctly over time. A single gauge reading only proves performance at the moment the mechanic happened to be standing there.

front: List the minimum contents required in a proper commissioning report.
back: At minimum a report needs the project and equipment identification, the date and outdoor conditions tests were performed under, every instrument used with its calibration date, the design values from the drawings and equipment schedule, the actual measured values, and a clear pass or fail determination against a stated tolerance for each test point. Photographs of nameplate data, gauge readings, and observed defects strengthen the report further.

front: Why does outdoor temperature at the time of testing matter enough to record in a commissioning report?
back: Capacity comparisons depend on the operating condition the system was tested under, and outdoor temperature directly affects that condition. Recording it lets anyone reviewing the report later judge whether the measured numbers should match full design load or a partial load condition.

front: What four pieces of information should every entry on a deficiency list include?
back: Each entry should describe the specific location, the nature of the deficiency, the trade responsible for correcting it, and a target date for resolution. A deficiency list is separate from the commissioning report but itemizes anything that does not meet design intent or code requirement.

front: Compare a vague deficiency entry to a properly written one for a disconnected flex duct connection at a rooftop unit.
back: A vague entry like "duct leaking somewhere near unit 3" gives almost nothing to act on.
