A proper entry states the specific location, the nature of the defect, and the impact, for example: flexible duct connection at RTU-3 supply, disconnected clamp, approximately 15 percent of measured design airflow lost, correction required before final balance can be verified.

front: A client questions months after handover whether a system was ever performing correctly. How does a proper commissioning report protect the mechanic?
back: A commissioning report with dated, instrument-verified readings is the mechanic's evidence that the system was performing to specification at the time of handover. Without that paper trail, a warranty or liability dispute becomes a matter of one party's word against the other's.

front: List the minimum topics client training should cover at handover.
back: Training should cover operating the thermostat or BAS interface for day-to-day adjustments, the routine maintenance schedule such as filter changes and belt inspection, what a normal versus an alarm condition looks like, and who to call for service versus what the operator can safely handle. The level of detail should be tailored to the audience.

front: Why should a mechanic walk a client through the O&M manual rather than just leaving it on a desk?
back: Assuming the manual will be read cover to cover is unrealistic, so the mechanic should point out where key information actually lives. This includes the location of shutoff valves and disconnects, warranty terms and what voids them, and the manufacturer's recommended maintenance intervals.

front: What four items make up a complete handover package at project close-out?
back: A complete handover package includes the commissioning report, the deficiency list with sign-off on completed corrections, the O&M manuals, and a training record showing who was trained and on what date. Together these close out the project professionally.

front: A facility operator has years of mechanical experience while an office manager mainly uses a thermostat. Should their handover training be identical?
back: No. Training should be tailored to the audience, so the mechanically experienced operator needs a deeper level of detail on system operation and maintenance than the office manager, who mainly needs to know normal thermostat use and who to call for service.

front: Why does treating client handover with the same care as technical fieldwork matter for a Red Seal mechanic's career?
back: A thorough, professional handover closes out the project cleanly and demonstrates competence beyond just the technical work. This builds the kind of reputation that generates repeat business and referrals, which matters as much in this trade as the ability to properly charge a system or balance a duct run.

front: Why does a written preventive maintenance schedule matter more than a one-time inspection?
back: A schedule assigns a task, a frequency, and an acceptable range of readings so every visit can be compared against a baseline. This lets a technician see drift toward failure before it actually fails. Without a baseline, every visit is a fresh guess instead of a trend.

front: What are the typical filter inspection and replacement intervals for a commercial rooftop unit versus a residential system?
back: A commercial rooftop unit typically needs monthly filter inspection and replacement every one to three months. A residential fibreglass filter is usually checked every one to two months. Dusty or greasy environments like restaurants and sawmills shorten these intervals considerably.

front: How does a dirty condenser coil affect head pressure and compressor amperage?
back: A condenser coil caked with dust, cottonwood fluff, or grass clippings cannot reject heat efficiently. This drives head pressure and compressor amperage up together. Coils should be inspected each visit and cleaned at least once a year, twice in high-debris locations.

front: How does a dirty or biologically fouled evaporator coil affect system performance?
back: A coil coated in dust or biological growth loses heat transfer surface area. This starves the refrigerant of the heat it needs to boil off inside the coil. The reduced heat transfer lowers cooling capacity even though airflow may still seem adequate at a glance.

front: Why can a slack drive belt cause airflow problems that are not visually obvious?
back: A belt that has stretched and gone slack slips under load, cutting airflow. There is no obvious visual sign until the belt is actually touched and deflected by hand. This applies to any unit using a belt-driven blower or belt-driven condenser fan.

front: Why are bearing checks for play, noise, and lubrication part of a preventive maintenance visit?
back: A seized bearing can lock a motor shaft and burn out the windings within minutes. Checking bearings on a set schedule catches wear before it causes a sudden, expensive failure. This applies to both blower motors and condenser fan motors.

front: Trace the failure chain that starts from a single skipped filter change.
back: A dirty filter causes low airflow, low airflow causes a cold or frosted evaporator coil, and a frosted coil restricts airflow further in a feedback loop. Eventually liquid refrigerant reaches the compressor. What starts as a cheap filter becomes a compressor replacement if the chain is not broken early.

front: Discharge pressure and saturation temperature sit above the expected condensing temperature for the ambient. What fault is this, and what causes it?
back: This is a high head pressure fault, which almost always points to a condenser that cannot reject heat properly. Common causes are a dirty or blocked condenser coil, a failed or slow condenser fan motor, condenser air recirculation, an overcharged system, or non-condensable gases from a poor evacuation. Suction side readings usually stay closer to normal unless the fault has progressed far enough to affect the whole circuit.

front: What does a preventive maintenance contract typically include, and how does it benefit both the client and the contractor?
back: A contract covers a fixed number of visits per year with a defined task list for each visit. The client gets predictable costs and fewer emergency failures. The contractor gets steady work and the chance to catch small issues during a planned visit instead of an emergency call.

front: List the common causes of low suction pressure on a vapour compression system.
back: Common causes are a low refrigerant charge, a restricted metering device, a plugged filter drier, a frozen evaporator coil, or low airflow across the evaporator. All of these reduce the mass of refrigerant reaching the compressor, so suction pressure drops. The technician narrows the cause by checking subcooling and looking for a temperature drop across the drier and metering device.

front: How does a technician distinguish a low refrigerant charge from a restriction when suction pressure is low?
back: Low subcooling combined with low suction pressure suggests an undercharge. A restriction is confirmed instead by inspecting the drier and metering device for a temperature drop across them, since a restriction causes that drop even when the charge itself is correct. Both checks are needed because low suction pressure alone does not separate the two.

front: What defines short cycling, and what is a normal compressor run cycle for comparison?
back: Short cycling is a compressor turning on and off far more often than its designed run cycle, every few minutes instead of a normal 10 to 20 minute cycle. It is hard on the compressor because the highest electrical stress happens at startup, and frequent starts multiply that stress over the unit's life. It always has an underlying cause that must be traced, not just accepted.

front: A compressor is short cycling every few minutes. What are the likely causes a technician should check?
back: Likely causes include an oversized unit for the load, a poorly placed thermostat that satisfies quickly, a dirty filter tripping a safety, a low pressure switch cutting out on marginal charge, or a failing run capacitor causing a hard start that trips the overload. Each cause is checked in turn since the symptom looks identical regardless of which one is present.

front: At what coil surface temperature does frost or ice begin to form on an evaporator, and what usually causes it?
back: Frost or ice forms when coil surface temperature drops below 0 degrees C for an extended period. The most common causes are low airflow, low charge, or a metering device feeding too little refrigerant to the coil. A dirty filter or blocked return is the single most common airflow cause.

front: What is the correct diagnostic order for tracing an evaporator frost or ice buildup complaint?
back: A technician checks airflow first, since a dirty filter or blocked return is the most common single cause. Suction pressure and superheat are checked next to separate an airflow-only problem from a charge or metering fault. Jumping straight to charge adjustment without checking airflow first risks masking the real problem.

front: For a frosted coil, what does low suction pressure with high superheat indicate, versus low suction pressure with normal superheat and good airflow?
back: Low suction pressure with high superheat suggests an undercharge or a restriction starving the coil of refrigerant. Low suction pressure with low or normal superheat, combined with confirmed good airflow, points toward an airflow problem alone rather than a charge or metering issue. Superheat is the key value that separates the two otherwise similar-looking symptoms.

front: Describe the pressure, temperature, and superheat signature of refrigerant flood-back to the compressor.
back: Flood-back shows low superheat, sometimes at or near zero, with a suction line cold and sweating well past the compressor inlet. In severe cases oil foaming is visible in a sight glass. This is the opposite pattern from a starved evaporator, which shows high superheat instead.

front: What conditions cause liquid refrigerant to flood back to the compressor?
back: Flood-back is caused by an overcharged system, a metering device stuck open, a failed or missing crankcase heater on a system prone to migration, or very low load conditions where the evaporator cannot boil off refrigerant fast enough. Any of these lets liquid reach the suction line instead of fully vaporized vapour.

front: What compressor damage results if refrigerant flood-back is left uncorrected?
back: Flood-back washes oil out of the compressor over time, robbing bearings of lubrication. It also causes liquid slugging, which damages bearings and valves directly on each stroke. Left long enough it condemns the compressor entirely.

front: Describe the pressure, temperature, and superheat signature of a starved evaporator.
back: A starved evaporator produces high superheat with a suction line that stays warm closer to the coil inlet. Cooling capacity is reduced even though the compressor runs, pulling low suction pressure as a result. This is the mirror image of flooding, which shows low superheat and higher suction pressure instead of high superheat and low suction pressure.

front: What causes an evaporator coil to be starved of refrigerant?
back: Causes include a plugged or undersized metering device, a plugged filter drier, a low charge, or a liquid line restriction such as a partially closed service valve. Any of these reduces the flow of refrigerant reaching the coil below what the load requires.

front: How does a technician confirm that an evaporator is starved rather than simply undercharged?
back: The technician measures temperature drop across the filter drier and the metering device. A healthy drier shows almost no measurable temperature drop across it, while a restricted one shows a marked drop. This pinpoints a physical restriction even when the overall system charge could otherwise appear correct.

front: A technician measures low suction pressure and unusually high superheat at the evaporator outlet. What fault does this point to?
back: This signature points to a starved evaporator, meaning too little refrigerant is reaching the coil. Likely causes are a plugged or undersized metering device, a plugged filter drier, a low charge, or a restricted liquid line. Confirming which one requires checking for a temperature drop across the drier and metering device.

front: A technician measures unusually high suction pressure with superheat near zero. What fault does this point to?
back: This signature points to refrigerant flooding back to the compressor rather than a starved coil. Likely causes are an overcharge, a metering device stuck open, a failed or missing crankcase heater, or very low load conditions. Left uncorrected this risks liquid slugging and bearing or valve damage.

front: What information should be logged on every preventive maintenance service record?
back: Each visit should log the date, readings taken including suction and discharge pressure, superheat, subcooling, and amperage draw, any refrigerant added or recovered with quantity and type, and any parts replaced. This lets the next technician see a trend line instead of a single snapshot. Complete records also document that leak repairs met regulatory reporting obligations.

front: Describe how a winding resistance test is performed on a de-energized compressor.
back: An ohmmeter is used across the common, run, and start terminals to check for a short, an open, or a ground fault. The unit must be de-energized and, ideally, refrigerant pressure equalized before testing. Readings between terminals are compared against the compressor's rated values.

front: What does an ohmmeter reading indicate if a compressor winding is shorted?
back: A short winding shows an abnormally low resistance reading between two terminals compared to rated values. This usually results from insulation breakdown due to overheating inside the winding. It is a condemning fault for that motor winding.

front: What does an ohmmeter reading indicate if a compressor winding is open?
back: An open winding shows infinite resistance, meaning no continuity, between two terminals that should read a specific value. This is most often caused by a burned-out winding or a blown overload that has not reset. The overload should be ruled out before condemning the winding itself.

front: How is a grounded compressor winding tested, and what does any continuity mean?
back: One meter lead is placed on any terminal and the other on the casing or a ground lug. Any continuity means the winding insulation has failed and is contacting the shell. This is a condemning fault on virtually every compressor.

front: A reciprocating compressor's motor runs and draws roughly normal amperage, but cooling capacity is poor. What mechanical fault should be suspected?
back: This points to mechanical valve failure, which shows reduced or no compression differential between suction and discharge even though the motor itself runs normally. It is most common on reciprocating compressor designs. A compression test is used to confirm the diagnosis.

front: How does a compression test distinguish healthy compressor valves from worn or broken valve reeds?
back: With the system isolated, a compressor with healthy valves pulls a strong vacuum on the suction side and builds discharge pressure quickly. A compressor with worn or broken valve reeds shows suction and discharge pressures pulling toward each other instead of separating. This happens because refrigerant leaks back past the damaged valve on each stroke.

front: What does a knocking or rattling noise from a running compressor typically indicate?
back: A knocking or rattling noise often indicates a broken or loose internal component, a worn connecting rod bearing, or liquid slugging from flood-back. The distinction usually requires checking suction line temperature and superheat to rule flood-back in or out. All three causes warrant shutting the unit down for further diagnosis.

front: What does a high-pitched whining or squealing noise under load suggest on a reciprocating versus a scroll compressor?
back: On either design it can point to a worn bearing. On a scroll compressor specifically it can also indicate worn scroll surfaces from lost lubrication or contamination. The noise pattern alone does not fully separate the two causes without further teardown or history review.

front: What does a hissing sound while a compressor is running indicate?
back: A hissing sound while running can indicate an internal bypass or a leaking discharge valve. Both allow high side gas to leak back internally rather than being fully delivered to the discharge line. This reduces capacity even without an obvious external symptom.

front: A compressor hums but does not start, then trips its overload. What causes should a technician suspect?
back: This usually indicates a failed start capacitor or start relay that is not bringing the start winding into the circuit. On a scroll compressor it can also mean the system was not equalized before restart, forcing the compressor to start against high head pressure. Both causes prevent the rotor from breaking away, so the motor draws locked rotor current until the overload trips.

front: How does an electronic leak detector locate a refrigerant leak in the field?
back: It uses a heated or infrared sensor that responds to halogenated refrigerant molecules in the air. These detectors are highly sensitive but also sensitive to airflow and contamination. The technician moves the probe slowly, close to the suspected joint, and confirms any alarm with a second pass after clearing drafts.

front: When is the soap bubble test most useful for confirming a refrigerant leak location?
back: It is most useful once the general area has been narrowed down, particularly during a standing pressure test with nitrogen on an as-yet uncharged system. A leak forms a visible bubble at the joint, giving precise visual confirmation an electronic sniffer alone cannot always provide. It works especially well on larger or hard-to-access fittings.

front: What makes UV dye detection effective for slow leaks that an electronic sniffer struggles to find?
back: Fluorescent dye is injected into the system, either at charging time or added later, and suspected areas are inspected with a UV lamp under black light. Any leak site shows a visible dye stain. This is effective for slow leaks that would take too long to build enough concentration for a sniffer, and for leaks hard to sniff directly, such as inside a coil bank.

front: What is the correct repair and verification sequence after a refrigerant leak is located and fixed?
back: A leaking flare or mechanical joint may only need re-torquing or a new flare, while a pinhole leak in tubing or a coil requires brazing. Any repair on a system that has held refrigerant should then be followed by a standing pressure test with nitrogen, then evacuation, then recharge. It should never simply be topped up over an unconfirmed repair.

front: Why is refrigerant leak diagnosis both a technical and a regulatory obligation in Canada?
back: Every refrigeration circuit is designed to be sealed for life, so any measurable loss of charge indicates a leak that must be located and repaired, not just topped up. Canadian federal and provincial regulations require leaks above certain thresholds to be repaired and documented. This makes proper diagnosis and record keeping a compliance requirement, not just good practice.

front: What symptoms does a run capacitor that has failed weak produce on a compressor or fan motor?
back: A run capacitor that has failed weak shows reduced motor performance and higher than normal running amperage. Sometimes the motor overheats over time as a result. The failure is gradual, so amperage trending over several visits can catch it before a hard failure.

front: What capacitance meter tolerance is used to judge whether a run capacitor or a start capacitor is still good?
back: A run capacitor should read within about six percent of its rated microfarad value. A start capacitor should read within about ten percent for most designs. A reading outside these tolerances means the capacitor should be condemned and replaced.

front: Besides a low capacitance reading, what physical signs condemn a capacitor on sight?
back: A capacitor that is visibly bulged, split, or leaking oil is condemned regardless of what a capacitance meter reads. Replacement must match the original rating and voltage class exactly. Using a mismatched capacitor can damage the motor it is protecting.

front: What causes contactor pitting, and what symptoms does it produce?
back: Pitting is a mechanical wear problem caused by repeated arcing across the contact points every cycle. Pitted contacts show visible burning or roughness and can cause intermittent operation or heat buildup from increased resistance. It is a normal wear pattern that worsens gradually over the contactor's life.

front: Why is a welded contactor considered a safety hazard, and what should a technician check after replacing one?
back: A welded contactor has fused contacts, so the load stays energized even with the coil de-energized, meaning the compressor or fan will not shut off with the thermostat. Any welded contactor is replaced immediately. The technician should also check for the underlying cause, often a locked rotor condition or severe short cycling that caused repeated high-current arcing.

front: What are the two distinct ways a failed start relay can affect a single-phase compressor?
back: A failed start relay may prevent the start capacitor from dropping out of the circuit, overheating the capacitor and causing it to fail too. It may instead fail to bring the start winding into the circuit at all, leaving the compressor humming without starting. Diagnosis checks relay contacts for continuity in both the energized and de-energized state, plus pickup and dropout voltage against specification.

front: What symptoms result when a thermostatic expansion valve is stuck open?
back: A TXV stuck open floods the evaporator with too much refrigerant regardless of load. The symptoms are identical to the flood-back signature: low superheat, a cold suction line well past the coil, and possible liquid slugging risk. The valve itself, not the charge, is the root cause here.

front: What symptoms result when a thermostatic expansion valve is stuck closed or nearly closed?
back: A TXV stuck closed produces the opposite of a stuck-open valve: high superheat, a starved evaporator, and reduced capacity. Frost may be limited to the coil inlet rather than spread evenly across the coil. This is the metering-device version of a starved evaporator fault.

front: How does a technician confirm that a TXV is mechanically stuck rather than simply misadjusted?
back: The technician checks the bulb charge and mounting, and checks for a plugged external equalizer line if the valve uses one. Then the adjustment is turned while observing whether superheat responds at all. Zero response to adjustment means the valve is mechanically stuck, not simply misadjusted.

front: A compressor shuts down under what appear to be normal operating pressures. How is a faulty high pressure switch confirmed as the cause?
back: A faulty high pressure switch trips prematurely, below its rated cutout, and is often mistaken for a genuine high head pressure fault. The technician confirms this by gauging actual discharge pressure at the moment of trip and comparing it against the switch's stamped setting. If actual pressure is well below the stamped cutout, the switch itself is at fault.

front: Why might a low pressure switch trip during a normal startup pulldown even though the system charge is correct?
back: A faulty low pressure switch behaves the same way as a faulty high pressure switch, tripping prematurely on the suction side. This can happen on a normal pulldown dip at startup if the switch's differential is set too tight or the switch has drifted out of calibration. Confirming this requires comparing actual suction pressure at trip against the switch's stamped setting.

front: How does thermostat calibration drift show up in the field, and how is it confirmed?
back: The thermostat's actual switching temperature moves away from its displayed setpoint over time, often from a failing sensor or a worn bimetal element on mechanical thermostats. It shows up as a space running consistently warmer or cooler than the display suggests. It is confirmed by comparing a calibrated reference thermometer near the sensor against the displayed reading over a full cycle.

front: How does scale buildup inside a water-to-refrigerant heat exchanger affect a water-source or geothermal system?
back: Scale buildup reduces heat transfer the same way a dirty coil does on an air-source unit. Hard water regions need periodic acid flushing or chemical descaling on a schedule set by local water hardness. Left unaddressed, scale gradually reduces capacity and increases energy use.

front: Why must loop flow rate on a water-source or geothermal system be verified against manufacturer specification?
back: Low flow reduces heat transfer and can trip a low temperature safety, shutting the unit down. Excessive flow wastes pump energy without improving performance. A flow meter or a temperature-differential calculation across the heat exchanger confirms actual flow against design.

front: What happens if antifreeze concentration in a closed-loop geothermal system drifts too low or too high?
back: Concentration too low risks freezing and rupturing the loop piping. Concentration too high reduces heat transfer efficiency and increases pumping energy. Concentration should be tested periodically since it can drift from leaks, dilution, or evaporation at fill points.

front: A heat pump blows cold air indoors for an extended period and never returns to heating mode. What defrost fault does this suggest?
back: This suggests the unit is stuck in defrost, usually from a defrost termination sensor that has failed open or misreads a warmer than actual temperature, or a control board that fails to time out the cycle. The indoor coil acts as the condenser during defrost, so cold air blows indoors until the cycle ends or auxiliary heat covers the load. A failed auxiliary stage on top of a stuck defrost leaves the space cold.

front: A heat pump's outdoor coil shows heavy visible frost or ice, but the unit never enters defrost. What should a technician check?
back: Likely causes are a failed defrost initiation sensor, a defrost timer or board that fails to trigger its scheduled check, or a reversing valve that has failed and cannot shift into defrost mode even when commanded. The technician confirms reversing valve function by manually forcing defrost through the control board's test function. A proper shift shows the expected pressure and temperature change across the valve.

front: A technician hears compressor knocking and finds a cold sweating suction line past the inlet, plus oil foaming in the sight glass. What is happening?
back: This is refrigerant flood-back causing liquid slugging inside the compressor, which risks bearing and valve damage. The technician should check for an overcharge, a metering device stuck open, a failed or missing crankcase heater, or very low load conditions. The unit should be shut down and the cause corrected before the compressor is damaged further.

front: What federal law governs refrigerant handling in Canada, and which agency enforces it?
back: Refrigerant handling falls under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 (CEPA). Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) administers CEPA and enforces the Ozone-depleting Substances and Halocarbon Alternatives Regulations under its authority. These regulations cover CFCs, HCFCs like R-22, and the HFC blends and halocarbon alternatives that replaced them.

front: State the core prohibition under ECCC's Ozone-depleting Substances and Halocarbon Alternatives Regulations.
back: Deliberate release of a controlled refrigerant to the atmosphere, called venting, is prohibited. Recovery is required whenever a refrigeration or air conditioning system is serviced, repaired, or decommissioned, regardless of system size or refrigerant amount.

front: Besides opening a valve on purpose, what other actions count as prohibited venting?
back: Avoidable losses from careless practice also count as venting under whichever regulation applies to the job, provincial for most private-sector work or the Federal Halocarbon Regulations for federal and Indigenous land equipment. Examples include disconnecting a charged hose without recovering the refrigerant trapped inside it, and abandoning a system with a known leak instead of isolating and repairing it.

front: Who can be held liable when a technician vents refrigerant, even by accident through negligent practice?
back: Both the technician and the employer can be held liable. The technician can face individual liability for the negligent practice, and the employer can face separate penalties for failing to maintain compliant procedures. These two responsibilities run side by side rather than one substituting for the other.

front: Besides the venting prohibition itself, what other technical requirements does ECCC set for recovery work?
back: ECCC's regulations also set technical requirements for recovery equipment, minimum recovery efficiency levels for different circuit configurations, and record keeping duties. A technician who knows only the venting prohibition and not this procedural detail will miss exam questions on the mechanics of compliance.

front: Why does the recovery requirement apply even on a very small refrigerant charge?
back: The applicable regulation, whether the provincial rule covering most private-sector work or the Federal Halocarbon Regulations for federal and Indigenous land equipment, requires recovery whenever a system is serviced, repaired, or decommissioned, regardless of system size or refrigerant amount. The federal Ozone-depleting Substances and Halocarbon Alternatives Regulations instead control manufacture, import, and export nationally. There is no minimum charge threshold that exempts a job from the recovery duty.

front: Which international treaty is the source of Canada's domestic refrigerant venting and recovery rules?
back: Canada is a party to the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer. Canada implemented its Montreal Protocol commitments through CEPA and the Ozone-depleting Substances and Halocarbon Alternatives Regulations.

front: What substances did the original Montreal Protocol target, and on what basis?
back: The original Montreal Protocol targeted ozone depleting substances, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and later hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs). It set a phase-down and eventual phase-out schedule for their production and consumption among member countries, based on their ozone-depleting impact.

front: What is the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol, and when was it adopted?
back: The Kigali Amendment, adopted in 2016, extended the Montreal Protocol's reach to cover hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). HFCs do not deplete the ozone layer, but many common HFC blends carry a high Global Warming Potential, so Kigali targets their climate impact instead. Canada ratified the Kigali Amendment and is bound by its schedule.

front: Is the Kigali Amendment an instant ban on HFCs, or does it work differently?
back: The Kigali Amendment is a phase-down mechanism, not an instant ban. Each party country gets a baseline level of HFC production and consumption expressed in CO2-equivalent terms, and that allowance is reduced in a series of steps over successive years, shrinking the total legal HFC volume.

front: What practical effect does the Kigali HFC phase-down have on refrigerants like R-404A and R-410A?
back: The phase-down causes a steady, ongoing reduction in legal supply and a corresponding rise in cost for high GWP HFC refrigerants such as R-404A and R-410A. Availability of newer lower GWP alternatives, including HFO blends and A2L refrigerants, grows in parallel.

front: Should a journeyperson expect a single cutover date away from legacy high GWP refrigerants?
back: No. The Kigali phase-down is a gradual, multi-year process, so a journeyperson should expect to service a mixed fleet of legacy high GWP systems and newer low GWP systems for a long transition period rather than one cutover date.

front: What class of refrigerant is R-22, and what is its current production status in Canada?
back: R-22 is an HCFC, and HCFCs were targeted by the original Montreal Protocol schedule for developed countries like Canada. New production and import of R-22 for use in Canada has already been phased out. This is a settled fact, not a future event.

front: Explain why the R-22 phase-out should not be confused with the Kigali HFC phase-down.
back: The R-22 phase-out targets an HCFC under the original Montreal Protocol schedule, which is already complete for new production and import. The Kigali Amendment is a separate, later mechanism that targets a different chemical family, HFCs, through an ongoing phase-down rather than a completed phase-out.

front: What are the only legal sources of R-22 for a system that still needs servicing?
back: The only legal sources are recovered R-22 reprocessed to at least the recycled standard, or reclaimed R-22 processed to a purity specification equivalent to new product. No newly manufactured R-22 may be imported or produced for use in Canada.

front: Why should recovered R-22 be kept in cylinders segregated from other refrigerant streams?
back: R-22 supply is fixed and shrinking, so recovered R-22 has real resale value rather than being scrap. Keeping R-22 recovery cylinders separated from other refrigerant streams keeps the material uncontaminated and reclaimable, protecting its value and its usability.

front: Besides R-22, name two CFC refrigerants that are further along the same phase-out path.
back: R-12 and R-502 are CFC refrigerants further along the same phase-out path as R-22. They are essentially unavailable except through recovery, recycling, and reclamation channels, since new production has already stopped for the whole ozone depleting substance family on its fixed schedule.

front: How is environmental protection jurisdiction for refrigerant handling divided in Canada?
back: Environmental protection is a shared jurisdiction, and for refrigerant recovery and venting the provinces do most of the actual work. The federal Ozone-depleting Substances and Halocarbon Alternatives Regulations control manufacture, import, and export nationally, and the separate Federal Halocarbon Regulations cover venting and recovery only for federal and Indigenous land equipment. For nearly all private-sector jobs, each province and territory enacts and enforces its own halocarbon or environmental protection regulation requiring recovery and prohibiting venting.

front: What does holding trade certification, provincially or through the Red Seal program, actually authorize?
back: Trade certification authorizes a technician personally to perform refrigerant handling work at a competent, trained standard. It demonstrates training in recovery procedures, cylinder handling, and the regulatory obligations that govern refrigerant work, and it operates alongside the employer's own compliance program rather than replacing it.

front: List employer-side responsibilities that must accompany a certified technician's compliance work.
back: The employer must maintain certified recovery equipment, provide correctly rated and labelled cylinders, keep the shop's refrigerant purchase and disposal records, and ensure technicians actually follow their trained procedures. A fully certified technician can still work in a non-compliant shop if the equipment is unmaintained or paperwork is not kept.

front: Define recovery in the context of refrigerant handling.
back: Recovery is the act of removing refrigerant from a system, in any condition, and storing it in an external container without necessarily testing or processing it. Recovered refrigerant may still contain moisture, acid, oil, or non-condensable gases.

front: Why is recovery described as the mandatory first step common to every refrigerant handling path?
back: Every time a system is opened for service, refrigerant must first be removed and stored externally before any further processing decision is made. Whether the gas is later recycled, reclaimed, or otherwise handled, recovery always happens first.

front: Define recycling as it applies to recovered refrigerant, and describe the equipment typically used.
back: Recycling reduces contamination in recovered refrigerant through oil separation, moisture removal with a filter drier, and single or multiple pass filtration. It is usually performed with equipment on site at the job or in the shop, rather than at a specialized facility.

front: What is the reuse limitation on recycled refrigerant compared to reclaimed refrigerant?
back: Recycled refrigerant is cleaned enough to be reused in the same system, or in other equipment owned by the same customer, but it does not meet the full purity standard required for resale as new refrigerant. Recycling is a lower bar meant for closed loop reuse, not general resale.

front: Define reclamation and the purity standard it must meet.
back: Reclamation is a full reprocessing of used refrigerant to the same purity specification as newly manufactured product, verified against a recognized chemical purity standard. It requires specialized equipment, typically a dedicated reclamation facility rather than field or shop equipment.

front: Why can reclaimed refrigerant legally be resold into a different customer's system, unlike recycled refrigerant?
back: Reclaimed refrigerant has been fully reprocessed to the same purity specification as new product and verified against a recognized purity standard. That full interchangeability lets it be legally resold into any compatible system, including systems belonging to other customers, unlike recycled refrigerant.

front: How does reclamation keep a phased out refrigerant like R-22 available for ongoing service?
back: Reclaimed material is treated as equivalent to new product for regulatory purposes because it meets the same purity specification. This lets reclaimed R-22 legally substitute for new production, which is otherwise unavailable, keeping existing R-22 systems serviceable.

front: What is a recovery machine, and how does its function differ from the refrigeration system itself?
back: A recovery machine is a dedicated compressor and condenser package built to pull refrigerant out of a customer's system and push it into a separate recovery cylinder. It removes and stores refrigerant rather than circulating it the way the system's own compressor does.

front: Compare vapour recovery and liquid recovery, and explain why liquid recovery is faster on large charges.
back: Vapour recovery draws off refrigerant vapour and condenses it inside the recovery machine, while liquid recovery removes refrigerant in its liquid state. Liquid recovery is faster on systems holding a larger charge because liquid removal moves far more mass per minute than vapour removal.

front: Before starting a recovery machine, what must a technician confirm about the recovery cylinder?
back: The technician connects the recovery machine between the system's service ports and an evacuated, correctly rated, properly labelled recovery cylinder. Gauges must confirm the cylinder is not already full past its allowable fill limit before recovery begins.

front: How should a technician judge when a recovery is actually complete?
back: The technician watches system side pressure and pulls down to a specified vacuum level appropriate to the refrigerant and equipment type, rather than stopping on a timer. A system left with residual refrigerant pressure after recovery is not actually recovered.

front: Why is refrigerant left in hoses before disconnection a compliance and safety concern?
back: Refrigerant remaining in hoses after recovery can be vented by accident when a fitting is cracked open. A careless technician who disconnects a charged hose without recovering the trapped refrigerant is committing a form of prohibited venting.

front: Describe push-pull recovery and the type of system where it is most commonly used.
back: Push-pull recovery uses the recovery machine's own compressor to pull vapour off the recovery cylinder and push it into the system, forcing liquid refrigerant out of the system's liquid receiver and into the recovery cylinder under the resulting pressure differential. It is common on larger commercial systems, where straight vapour or liquid recovery alone would take too long.

front: After recovering refrigerant from a system, what should a technician confirm the quantity against?
back: The technician must weigh or otherwise confirm how much refrigerant was recovered against the equipment's nameplate charge. This verifies the recovery was complete and provides accurate data for the compliance documentation the shop must keep.

front: Are recovery cylinders treated as disposable containers under transport and safety rules?
back: No. Recovery cylinders are refillable pressure vessels, treated as such under transport and pressure vessel safety rules. They are reused across many recovery jobs rather than discarded after one fill.

front: Describe the conventional colour scheme for a North American recovery cylinder and how it differs from a new disposable cylinder.
back: A recovery cylinder is conventionally painted grey with a yellow shoulder or top. New, disposable refrigerant-specific cylinders use different colours, for example R-410A cylinders are typically rose-coloured and R-22 cylinders are light green.

front: Since a grey-and-yellow recovery cylinder is a mixed-use container, how must it be identified between different refrigerant uses?
back: The cylinder must carry a legible label stating whatever refrigerant it currently holds, rather than being identified by tank colour alone. One recovery cylinder may serve different refrigerants across its service life, provided it is fully evacuated and correctly relabelled between uses.

front: Which Canadian regulatory framework governs refillable refrigerant recovery cylinders, and what physical rating do they carry?
back: Refillable recovery cylinders fall under Transport Canada's Transportation of Dangerous Goods (TDG) requirements, which mirror the DOT specification framework used in the United States. The physical cylinder commonly carries a DOT-4BA or DOT-4BW type rating stamped into it, setting its maximum working pressure and safe fill limit. A DOT-39 rating marks a non-refillable, single-trip cylinder and must never be refilled or used as a recovery cylinder.

front: How often must a standard DOT-4BA/4BW recovery cylinder undergo hydrostatic requalification testing, and what happens if it is overdue?
back: A standard DOT-4BA or DOT-4BW type cylinder typically requires hydrostatic requalification at a five-year interval, stamped with the test date on the cylinder. A cylinder outside its requalification window cannot legally be filled or transported, and using it is both a regulatory violation and a real safety hazard. DOT-39 cylinders are non-refillable, single-trip containers that are never requalified or refilled.

front: Describe the letter-and-number safety group system used to classify refrigerants by toxicity and flammability.
back: A letter indicates toxicity, A for lower toxicity and B for higher toxicity. A number indicates flammability: 1 means no flame propagation, 2L means mildly flammable, 2 means flammable, and 3 means higher flammability.

front: What safety classification do R-410A and R-22 carry, and what does that classification mean?
back: R-410A and R-22 are classified A1. That means both refrigerants have lower toxicity and show no flame propagation under standard test conditions.

front: Name two A2L refrigerants that have entered common use under the Kigali low GWP shift.
back: R-32 and R-454B are A2L refrigerants that have entered common use. Their adoption is part of the industry-wide shift toward lower GWP options driven by the Kigali Amendment's HFC phase-down.

front: What does the 2L designation mean for the burning behaviour of a refrigerant like R-32?
back: The 2L designation means the refrigerant is mildly flammable. It will burn under specific conditions, but it has a low burning velocity and requires a higher concentration in air plus a real ignition source to sustain combustion.

front: How does an A2L refrigerant's risk category compare to a fully flammable A2 or A3 refrigerant such as propane (R-290)?
back: A2L refrigerants sit in a distinct, lower-risk category than fully flammable A2 or A3 refrigerants like propane (R-290). Mild flammability under specific conditions is a lower hazard than the fuller flammability of the A2 or A3 class.

front: What must be true of recovery machines and leak detectors used on an A2L refrigerant system?
back: Service equipment used on A2L systems must be rated for mildly flammable refrigerants. Standard A1-only equipment lacks the spark-free components and enclosure ratings needed to safely handle a refrigerant that can ignite.

front: What storage and ventilation factor becomes important with A2L refrigerants that is less relevant with A1 refrigerants?
back: Storage areas and shop ventilation must account for a refrigerant accumulation reaching a flammable concentration in an enclosed space. This matters particularly at floor level, since A2L refrigerant is heavier than air and can pool there.

front: What must a technician do before brazing on a charged A2L refrigerant line?
back: The line requires full evacuation and purging before any brazing or other hot work. Brazing directly on a charged A2L line, something a technician might do without a second thought on an A1 system, introduces a real ignition risk.

front: What design consideration applies to electrical enclosures near a possible A2L leak point?
back: Electrical enclosures and other system components near a possible A2L leak point should carry flammable-refrigerant-rated designs from the manufacturer. This reduces the chance of an ignition source being present where a mildly flammable refrigerant could accumulate.

front: How is a system losing refrigerant at an elevated rate over a service interval treated under this framework?
back: It is treated as a compliance problem, not just a performance problem. A leak rate above the threshold that applies to that system's size and type calls for repairing the leak and confirming the repair, rather than simply topping up the charge.

front: Why does repeatedly recharging a leaking system without repairing it defeat the purpose of the recovery and venting rules?
back: Every top up on an unrepaired leaking system effectively feeds a slow, unauthorized release to atmosphere. This undermines the entire purpose of the recovery and venting rules even though no single event looks like deliberate venting.

front: How must refrigerant that cannot be recycled or reclaimed, and contaminated recovered oil, be handled for disposal?
back: Both must be handled as regulated waste rather than disposed of through ordinary channels. This means using a licensed waste handler or refrigerant reclaimer, keeping material properly labelled and contained until pickup, and never disposing of either down a drain or into general waste.

front: What records should a compliant service company keep to demonstrate refrigerant accountability?
back: Records should cover refrigerant purchases, the quantity recovered from each job matched against the system's original charge, refrigerant sent for recycling or reclamation, and the final disposition of any refrigerant or cylinder leaving the shop. These records show refrigerant is accounted for with no unexplained gap suggesting undocumented venting.

front: What specific information should a technician record on a service ticket to support the shop's compliance record?
back: A technician should record cylinder weight in and out, the refrigerant type, and the job reference on every service ticket. This front-line record keeping is what makes the shop's overall compliance documentation possible.

front: Who is the intended audience for a service company's refrigerant record keeping, and what gap are the records meant to rule out?
back: An inspector or auditor is exactly who will ask to see these records. Complete records rule out an unexplained gap between refrigerant purchased and refrigerant accounted for, which would otherwise suggest undocumented venting.

front: Why must every independent refrigeration circuit be recovered before decommissioning a piece of equipment?
back: Decommissioning carries the same recovery obligation as any other service call, and the full refrigerant charge must be recovered from every circuit before cutting, crushing, or disposal. Some equipment has multiple independent refrigeration circuits or a pump-down receiver holding charge separately from the rest of the system.

front: During decommissioning, what should a technician do if the recovered quantity falls significantly short of the nameplate charge?
back: The technician should confirm the recovered quantity against the equipment's nameplate charge where possible and investigate any significant shortfall, rather than assuming the missing refrigerant simply was not there. A large shortfall can indicate a long-standing undetected leak that itself needs documenting.

front: What must happen before a decommissioned system moves on to demolition or scrap processing, and how should its compressor oil be handled?
back: Once recovery is confirmed complete, the equipment can be tagged refrigerant-free before demolition, recycling, or scrap processing, protecting downstream workers from handling a pressurized system as inert scrap metal. Compressor oil should be drained and handled as contaminated waste, since it typically retains dissolved refrigerant.
